title: Book Four (1806) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: Rostov's involvement in Dolokhov's duel with Bezukhov was smoothed over through the efforts of old Count Rostov, and instead of being demoted to the ranks as he'd expected, Nicholas was appointed adjutant to the governor-general of Moscow. As a result, he couldn't go to the country with the rest of the family and was kept in Moscow all summer by his new duties. Dolokhov recovered, and Rostov grew very close to him during his convalescence. Dolokhov lay ill at his mother's home — she loved him passionately and tenderly — and old Mary Ivanovna, who had taken a liking to Rostov because of his friendship with her Fedya, often talked to him about her son.

"Yes, Count," she would say, "he is too noble and pure-hearted for this depraved world of ours. Nobody values virtue anymore — it seems like a reproach to everyone. Now tell me, Count — was it right, was it honorable, what Bezukhov did? And Fedya, with his noble spirit, loved him and still doesn't say a word against him. Those pranks in Petersburg when they played tricks on a policeman — didn't they do it together? And look! Bezukhov got off without a scratch while Fedya had to shoulder the whole burden. Think what he went through! Yes, he's been reinstated, but how could they not reinstate him? I doubt there were many sons of the fatherland out there as brave as he was. And now this duel! Have these people no sense of decency or honor? Knowing he's an only son, to challenge him and shoot so accurately! Thank God He had mercy on us. And what was it all about? Who doesn't have affairs these days? If he was so jealous — to my mind — he should have said something sooner, instead of letting it go on for months. And then to challenge him, counting on Fedya not fighting because he owed him money! How low! How contemptible! I know you understand Fedya, my dear Count — and believe me, that's why I'm so fond of you. Very few people truly understand him. He has such a noble, heavenly soul!"
Dolokhov himself, during his recovery, spoke to Rostov in a way no one would have expected.

"I know people think I'm a bad man!" he said. "Let them! I don't care about anyone except those I love. But the people I love, I love so fiercely I'd give my life for them — and everyone else I'd crush if they got in my way. I have a wonderful, priceless mother and two or three friends — you among them — and as for the rest, they only matter to me insofar as they're harmful or useful. And most of them are harmful, especially the women. Yes, my friend," he went on, "I've met loving, noble, high-minded men, but I've never yet met a woman — whether countess or kitchen maid — who wasn't mercenary. I haven't found that divine purity and devotion I look for in a woman. If I found someone like that, I'd give my life for her! But these..." and he made a gesture of contempt. "And believe me, if I still value my life, it's only because I still hope to find such a heavenly creature — someone who will transform, purify, and lift me up. But you don't understand that."
"Oh yes, I understand completely," answered Rostov, who was now fully under his new friend's influence.

In the autumn the Rostovs returned to Moscow. Early in the winter Denisov arrived too and stayed with them. The first half of the winter of 1806, which Nicholas Rostov spent in Moscow, was one of the happiest and most carefree times for him and the whole family. Nicholas brought many young men home to his parents' house. Vera was a striking girl of twenty; Sonya was a girl of sixteen with all the charm of a flower just opening; Natasha — half grown-up and half child — was sometimes childishly amusing, sometimes enchantingly girlish.

At that time the Rostov household was filled with the kind of romantic atmosphere typical of homes where there are very young and very charming girls. Every young man who visited — seeing those responsive, smiling young faces (smiling, no doubt, at their own happiness), feeling the eager energy around him, and hearing the bursts of song and music and the lighthearted, open chatter of girls ready for anything and full of hope — felt the same thing: a shared readiness to fall in love and an expectation that happiness was just around the corner.

Among the young men Nicholas brought to the house, one of the first was Dolokhov, whom everyone liked except Natasha. She nearly quarreled with her brother over him. She insisted that he was a bad person, that Pierre had been in the right in the duel and Dolokhov in the wrong, and furthermore that he was disagreeable and fake.

"There's nothing to understand," she declared with stubborn conviction. "He's cruel and heartless. Look — I like your Denisov, even though he's a wild one and all that — I still like him. So you see, I can judge people. But with this one, everything is calculated, and I don't like that. But Denisov..."

"Oh, Denisov is completely different," replied Nicholas, implying that even Denisov was nothing compared to Dolokhov. "You need to understand what kind of soul Dolokhov has — you should see him with his mother. What a heart!"
"Well, I don't know about all that, but I'm uncomfortable around him. And did you know he's fallen in love with Sonya?"

Natasha's prediction turned out to be right. Dolokhov, who normally didn't seek out women's company, began visiting the house frequently, and the question of whom he was coming to see — though nobody spoke of it openly — was soon answered. He came for Sonya. And Sonya, though she would never have dared say it aloud, knew it and blushed bright red every time Dolokhov appeared.

Dolokhov often dined at the Rostovs', never missed a performance they attended, and went to Iogel's dance parties for young people, which the Rostovs always frequented. He was pointedly attentive to Sonya and looked at her in a way that made not only her blush but even the old countess and Natasha turn red when they noticed his gaze.
It was obvious that this strange, powerful man was under the irresistible spell of the dark, graceful girl who loved someone else.

Rostov noticed something new in Dolokhov's behavior toward Sonya, but he didn't try to figure out what these new dynamics meant. "They're always falling in love with somebody," he thought about Sonya and Natasha. But he wasn't as comfortable around Sonya and Dolokhov as before, and he spent less time at home.

In the autumn of 1806, talk of war with Napoleon had flared up again, even more intensely than the year before. Orders went out to raise recruits — ten men from every thousand for the regular army, plus nine from every thousand for the militia. Bonaparte was denounced everywhere, and in Moscow nothing was talked about but the coming war. For the Rostov family, the real significance of all these war preparations was that Nicholas refused to stay in Moscow and was only waiting for Denisov's leave to end after Christmas so he could return with him to their regiment. His approaching departure didn't stop him from enjoying himself — if anything, it added urgency to his pleasures. He spent most of his time away from home, at dinners, parties, and balls.
